detections.evidence_quote: today's episode is all about understanding delusion and psychosis
detections.summary: Host explains delusion and psychosis, their closed-loop logic, definitions and distinctions.

detections.evidence_quote: Someone has an intrusive thought about doing something horrific
detections.summary: Host distinguishes intrusive thoughts from psychosis and promises a framework for telling them apart.

detections.evidence_quote: reality testing questions being labeled as narcissistic and gaslighting
detections.summary: Host discusses social-media mislabeling of reality testing as narcissism and gaslighting, and gray rocking.
Host corrects the interchangeability of intrusive thoughts and psychosis.

detections.evidence_quote: This is the first misconception: people believe things every single day that are inaccurate
detections.summary: Host corrects the misconception that believing inaccurate things is psychosis.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Having an intrusive thought about doing something horrific is not the same as being in psychosis.
verification_candidates.rationale: A common clinical distinction that affects whether intrusive thoughts are treated as psychosis.

verification_candidates.claim_text: A delusion involves a belief held with conviction that is resistant to contradictory evidence and disconnected from consensual reality.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Held with a level of conviction that is resistant to contradictory evidence and is disconnected from consensual reality
verification_candidates.rationale: A definitional claim about delusion that can be checked against clinical criteria.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Reality testing someone who is in delusion will make them more angry or emotionally aroused.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: reality testing to somebody who is in delusion will actually make them more angry
verification_candidates.rationale: A clinical-interaction claim that affects how people respond to someone in psychosis.

verification_candidates.claim_text: In many cases, the person who believes they are being gaslit is the one gaslighting the person trying to ask the right questions.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: the person who believes they're being gaslit is the one gaslighting the person who is desperately trying to ask the right questions
verification_candidates.rationale: A strong claim about gaslighting dynamics that could be examined or challenged.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Repeatedly misinterpreting others' words or expressions in a sustained manner could eventually lead to psychosis.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: although repeatedly in a sustained manner, that could eventually lead to psychosis
verification_candidates.rationale: A causal claim about progression from ordinary misperception to psychosis.
